content: Statins are medications primarily used to lower lipid levels, but they also have additional effects on metabolic and endocrine functions. In women with polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) who are not actively trying to conceive, statins have been proposed to not only address dyslipidemia but also potentially reduce testosterone levels and improve other metabolic parameters. This review aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of statin therapy in this population. The review included six randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 396 women with PCOS who underwent treatment for six weeks, three months, or six months. Of these, 374 participants completed the studies. Three trials investigated the effects of simvastatin, while the other three focused on atorvastatin. The findings were categorized into several comparisons: 1. Statins versus placebo (3 RCTs): One trial assessed menstrual regularity by measuring the length of the menstrual cycle. The evidence was very uncertain as to whether statins shortened the menstrual cycle compared to placebo (mean difference [MD] −2.00 days, 95% confidence interval [CI] −24.86 to 20.86; 37 participants; very low-certainty evidence). None of the studies reported on the resumption of spontaneous ovulation, improvement in hirsutism, or improvement in acne severity. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether statins reduced testosterone levels after six weeks (MD 0.06, 95% CI −0.72 to 0.84; 1 RCT, 20 participants), three months (MD −0.53, 95% CI −1.61 to 0.54; 2 RCTs, 64 participants), or six months (MD 0.10, 95% CI −0.43 to 0.63; 1 RCT, 28 participants). Two studies reported adverse events, but no significant differences were observed between the statin and placebo groups. 2. Statins plus metformin versus metformin alone (1 RCT): This trial measured menstrual regularity as the number of spontaneous menses over six months. The evidence was very uncertain as to whether the combination of statins and metformin improved menstrual regularity compared to metformin alone (MD 0.60 menses, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.12; 69 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The study did not report on the resumption of spontaneous ovulation. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether the combination improved hirsutism (MD −0.16, 95% CI −0.91 to 0.59; 69 participants), acne severity (MD −0.31, 95% CI −0.67 to 0.05; 69 participants), or testosterone levels (MD −0.03, 95% CI −0.37 to 0.31; 69 participants). No significant adverse events were reported. 3. Statins plus oral contraceptive pill (OCP) versus OCP alone (1 RCT): This trial did not report on menstrual regularity or spontaneous ovulation. The evidence was very uncertain as to whether the combination of statins and OCP improved hirsutism compared to OCP alone (MD −0.12, 95% CI −0.41 to 0.17; 48 participants). Acne severity was not reported. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether the combination reduced testosterone levels (MD −0.82, 95% CI −1.38 to −0.26; 48 participants). No significant adverse events were reported. 4. Statins versus metformin (2 RCTs): The evidence was very uncertain as to whether statins improved menstrual regularity compared to metformin (MD 0.50 menses, 95% CI −0.05 to 1.05; 1 RCT, 61 participants). None of the studies reported on the resumption of spontaneous ovulation. The evidence was very uncertain regarding whether statins reduced hirsutism (MD −0.26, 95% CI −0.97 to 0.45; 1 RCT, 61 participants), acne severity (MD −0.18, 95% CI −0.53 to 0.17; 1 RCT, 61 participants), or testosterone levels (MD −0.24, 95% CI −0.58 to 0.10; 1 RCT, 61 participants). Both trials reported no significant adverse events. 5. Statins versus oral contraceptive pill plus flutamide (1 RCT): No significant adverse events were reported. No data were available for any of the primary outcomes or other secondary outcomes. Conclusions: The evidence for all primary and secondary outcomes in this review was of very low certainty. It remains unclear whether statins, either alone or in combination with other agents, improve menstrual regularity, spontaneous ovulation, hirsutism, acne severity, or testosterone levels in women with PCOS who are not actively trying to conceive. All trials that assessed adverse events reported no significant differences between the groups. Further high-quality research is needed to clarify the role of statins in this population.
